title: Safe money that shrinks
topic: Why safe money can lose value

steps.title: Same money, less to buy
steps.body: Since 2020, prices in Germany have risen by about a fifth. In 2022 alone, they rose by almost 7%. This is called [[inflation]]. Your balance stays the same, but it buys less. What €10,000 bought in 2020 costs about €12,200 today.

steps.title: A basket of 650 things
steps.body: Statisticians follow the prices of about 650 kinds of goods and services that households buy: food, rent, energy, travel, haircuts. Inflation is how much more this basket costs than a year earlier. Not every price moves the same way: in 2022, energy rose far faster than clothes. The European Central Bank aims for about 2% a year. Money only keeps its value when it earns at least that. What it earns after inflation is its [[real-return]].

stat.label: the price rise the ECB aims for each year

steps.prompt: This basket holds what €100 buys today. Move the interest until the basket stays full after 10 years.

output.label: Change in what the money can buy

goal.hint: The interest has to be at least as high as the price rise.

steps.note: Try the price rise at 7%, like in 2022, and watch the basket empty.

steps.prompt: Myth or fact? Swipe each statement.

items.text: My balance never falls, so inflation cannot touch my money
At 2% inflation, money loses half its buying power in about 35 years
Inflation means every price rises by the same amount
Interest above inflation means your money buys more each year
Cash at home is the safest place when prices rise
The European Central Bank aims for about 2% inflation a year

steps.explanation: The number on the screen can stay the same while what it buys shrinks. Only interest above [[inflation]] keeps buying power growing.

steps.prompt: €10,000 is for a flat deposit in 3 years. Prices rise 2.5% a year. Where does it wait? Pick one, then jump 3 years ahead.

choices.label: On the current account, at 0%
choices.ending: The balance still says €10,000, but it buys what €9,286 buys today. Money with no interest loses to prices every year.

choices.label: In the savings account, at 2.25%
choices.ending: Almost even: the interest nearly keeps up with prices. The rate can change at any time, and the money is ready any day.

choices.label: In a fixed-term deposit, 3% fixed
choices.ending: The money buys a little more than today. The rate is fixed, but the money is locked until the end of the term. That fits money with a known date.

choices.label: In a stock fund
choices.ending: In this example it ends up ahead, but in year 2 it was down. Over 3 years a fund can just as well be down on the day you need the money. A short [[time-horizon]] leaves no time to wait.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 1 of 3 · What does an inflation rate of 3% mean?
options: On average, the basket of goods costs 3% more than a year ago
The bank takes 3% of your balance
steps.explanation: [[inflation]] is an average over a basket. Some prices rise much more, some less, some even fall.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 2 of 3 · Savings earn 2%. Prices rise 3%. What happens to what the money can buy?
options: It shrinks by about 1% a year
It stays the same, the balance never falls
steps.explanation: The [[real-return]] is the interest minus inflation: 2% − 3% ≈ −1%. The balance grows, the buying power shrinks.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 3 of 3 · Which money fits a fixed-term deposit?
options: Money you will not need until a known date
Money for a car repair next week
steps.explanation: A [[fixed-term-deposit]] pays a fixed rate but locks the money until the end. That suits money with a clear [[time-horizon]], not money for surprises.
